Cooking on Two Wheels

A hot meal and a fresh brew at camp after a long day's riding is one of motorcycle touring's greatest pleasures. You do not need elaborate cooking equipment — a compact stove, a pot, and a few basics let you prepare everything from morning coffee to evening pasta. The key is keeping the kit lightweight, compact, and reliable.

Stove Options

  • Canister stoves — Screw-on stoves using threaded gas canisters. Light, reliable, and easy to use. The flame is adjustable for simmering. Canisters are widely available at outdoor shops and larger petrol stations across the UK.
  • Integrated systems (JetBoil, MSR Windburner) — Stove and pot designed as one unit for maximum efficiency. They boil water incredibly fast and are very fuel-efficient. Slightly heavier and more expensive but excellent for riders who primarily want hot drinks and rehydrated meals.
  • Alcohol stoves — Ultra-lightweight with no moving parts. Fuel is cheap and available everywhere. Slower to boil and harder to control flame, but weighs almost nothing.
  • Solid fuel tablets — The lightest and simplest option. Fold-flat stove weighing under 50g. Very slow to boil but virtually indestructible and useful as an emergency backup.

Essential Cookware

Pot — A 750ml-1L titanium or aluminium pot with a lid handles all solo cooking needs. Titanium is lighter but aluminium distributes heat more evenly for cooking food rather than just boiling water.

Mug — A double-wall titanium mug keeps drinks hot without burning your hands. Many nest inside the pot for compact packing.

Spork — A combination spoon-fork handles all eating duties. Titanium or Lexan plastic versions weigh virtually nothing.

Lighter and matches — Always carry both. A windproof lighter is your primary ignition and waterproof matches are the backup.

Meal Ideas for Moto Camping

Breakfast: Porridge with dried fruit, coffee or tea. Instant porridge sachets are light, filling, and cook in two minutes. Pack ground coffee for a proper morning brew.

Lunch: Eat at a cafe or pub — part of the touring experience. If cooking, couscous with tuna is quick, nutritious, and requires only boiling water.

Dinner: Dehydrated camping meals have improved enormously. Brands like Firepot and Expedition Foods offer genuinely tasty freeze-dried meals that rehydrate in minutes. Alternatively, pasta with pesto and cheese is cheap, filling, and simple to cook. Read our Essential Motorcycle Camping Gear for UK Tours guide for more. Read our Lightweight Tents for Motorcycle Touring in the UK guide for more.

Never cook inside your tent. Carbon monoxide from gas stoves is deadly in enclosed spaces, and a knocked-over stove can ignite your tent fabric in seconds. Always cook in the vestibule with the door open or outside under a tarp.
keyTakeaways: A compact canister stove, a small pot and a mug cover almost all camp cooking needs.
Integrated systems like JetBoil boil water fastest; alcohol and solid-fuel stoves are lightest.
A 750ml to 1L titanium or aluminium pot handles all solo cooking.
Modern dehydrated meals from brands like Firepot rehydrate in minutes and taste genuinely good.
Never cook inside your tent; carbon monoxide is deadly and spilled fuel can ignite the fabric.

pros: A hot brew and meal at camp is one of touring's great pleasures.
Compact canister stoves are light, reliable and simple to use.
Canister gas is widely available at UK outdoor shops and larger fuel stations.
cons: Integrated systems are excellent for boiling but poor for real cooking.
Alcohol and solid-fuel stoves are slow and hard to control.
Fuel canisters add bulk and cannot be flown with if you tour abroad.

faq.q: What type of camp stove is best for motorcycle touring?
faq.a: A screw-on canister stove is the best all-rounder: light, reliable, easy to use and with an adjustable flame for simmering. Integrated systems like the JetBoil boil water incredibly fast and are very fuel-efficient, ideal if you mainly want hot drinks and dehydrated meals. Alcohol and solid-fuel stoves are lighter still but slower and harder to control.

faq.q: What cookware do I actually need?
faq.a: For solo touring, a 750ml to 1L titanium or aluminium pot with a lid covers all your cooking. Add a double-wall titanium mug that nests inside the pot, a spork and both a windproof lighter and waterproof matches. Titanium is lighter, while aluminium spreads heat more evenly for cooking food rather than just boiling water.

faq.q: What should I cook while motorcycle camping?
faq.a: Keep it simple. Instant porridge and ground coffee make a quick, filling breakfast. For dinner, modern dehydrated meals from brands like Firepot and Expedition Foods rehydrate in minutes and taste surprisingly good, or pasta with pesto and cheese is cheap and easy. Many riders eat lunch at a cafe or pub as part of the touring experience.

faq.q: Can I cook inside my tent if it is raining?
faq.a: No, never cook inside the inner tent. Carbon monoxide from a gas stove is deadly in an enclosed space, and a knocked-over stove can ignite the fabric in seconds. If it is raining, cook in the vestibule with the door open for ventilation, or under a separate tarp, keeping the flame well away from any tent material.

faq.q: Where can I buy gas canisters in the UK?
faq.a: Threaded canisters are widely available at outdoor shops such as Go Outdoors and Cotswold Outdoor, many supermarkets and even some larger petrol stations. Plan a resupply if you are on a long tour, and remember you cannot carry gas canisters on a flight, so buy them locally if your tour starts with a ferry or plane.
